ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the circuit diagram, the non-inverting input terminal (+) of the operational amplifier is grounded; the input signal Vi(jω) first passes through a resistor R and is connected to the summing node of the inverting input terminal; this summing node is also grounded through 2C and 2R respectively; the output terminal Vo(jω) is connected back to the same inverting node through a feedback network, and the feedback network is composed of resistor R and capacitor C connected in parallel. Reasoning: The op-amp is ideal and negative feedback exists, so the inverting input node is virtual ground, that is, the voltage is 0 V. Since the voltage between this node and ground is 0, the 2R and 2C branches connected from this node to ground have no current and can be ignored. The feedback impedance is Z_f = R || 1/(jωC) = R/(1+jωRC). The input resistance is R, therefore the transfer function Vo/Vi = -Z_f/R = -1/(1+jωRC), which is a first-order low-pass filter. Its -3 dB cutoff angular frequency satisfies ωRC = 1, so f_c = 1/(2πRC). Substituting R = 2 kΩ = 2000 Ω, C = 1 μF = 1e-6 F, RC = 0.002 s, therefore f_c = 1/(2π×0.002) = 79.58 Hz.

Apply the ideal op-amp virtual-ground condition at the inverting node. Since that node is at 0 V, the parallel branches 2R and 2C to ground carry no current and can be ignored. Compute the feedback impedance Z_f = R || 1/(j omega C) = R/(1+j omega RC). Thus V_o/V_i = -Z_f/R = -1/(1+j omega RC). The -3 dB point of this first-order low-pass occurs at omega RC = 1; substitute R = 2 kOhm and C = 1 microF to get f_c = 1/(2*pi*RC) = 79.58 Hz.
